tables.name: analytics_events

columns.name: id
columns.doc: Auto-incrementing primary key generated from analytics_events_id_seq.

columns.name: uid
columns.doc: Nullable reference to users.id representing the acting user, but not enforced by a foreign key so it can point to nonexistent or deleted users.

columns.name: event
columns.doc: Free-text event name with no enum or check constraint, making naming consistency entirely dependent on producers.

columns.name: props
columns.doc: Unstructured JSONB payload for event-specific properties with no schema enforcement, so structure may vary by event type or version.

columns.name: ts
columns.doc: Bigint epoch timestamp of the event with no documented unit (seconds vs milliseconds) or timezone, unlike a native timestamptz.

tables.doc: Stores generic product analytics events (event name + arbitrary JSON payload) keyed loosely to a user via 'uid'; currently a tiny, low-traffic table (~3 rows, 41 reads/day, 3 writes/day), suggesting it's either newly instrumented or only lightly used/tested. 'ts' is a bigint epoch timestamp rather than a native timestamp type, and 'uid' has no enforced foreign key to 'users', so referential integrity depends entirely on application code.
issues: uid -> users relationship is not enforced by a foreign key, allowing orphaned or invalid uid values
ts is stored as bigint (epoch) instead of a timestamp/timestamptz type, with no documented unit (seconds vs milliseconds) or timezone convention
event is a free-text column with no enum/check constraint, risking inconsistent naming (casing, typos, synonyms) across producers
uid, event, ts, and props are all nullable, so core fields needed to interpret an event (who, what, when) can be missing entirely
props is unconstrained jsonb with no schema validation, so payload shape can drift silently across event types or app versions

tables.name: feature_flags

columns.name: rollout
columns.doc: Optional JSON blob describing rollout targeting rules (e.g., percentage or user segments) with no enforced schema.

tables.doc: Stores feature flag definitions used to toggle application features on/off, with optional JSON-based rollout configuration (e.g., percentage or cohort targeting). Extremely low volume (2 rows, 1 read/day) suggests this is either a new/underused system or flags are cached elsewhere after being read; engineers should confirm whether the app actually queries this table at runtime or relies on a cache/env vars instead. No primary key is declared on 'flag', so uniqueness is not enforced by schema alone.
issues: No explicit primary key or unique constraint shown on 'flag', so duplicate flag names could be inserted
'enabled' is nullable, creating a three-state boolean (true/false/null) with unclear semantics for null — likely should default to false and be NOT NULL
'rollout' jsonb has no schema/shape validation, so structure can drift silently across the only 2 rows without anyone noticing
Very low read count (1/day) is suspicious for a feature flag table — may indicate flags are read once at boot and cached, meaning stale flags could persist until restart
No created_at/updated_at timestamps, so there's no audit trail for when a flag was toggled or added

tables.doc: order_items stores line items (product + quantity + price) for orders, linking to orders via order_id and to products via product_id; unit_price_cents captures price in integer cents at time of purchase. Currently empty (0 rows) with modest read traffic and zero writes, suggesting it is either newly created, unused, or being phased out in favor of a v2 pipeline. Critical: the enforced FK on order_id still points to the deprecated 'orders' table while live order data lives in 'orders_v2', so any new writes or joins against 'orders' will silently miss current orders.
issues: Enforced FK (order_id -> orders.id) targets a deprecated table; live orders are in orders_v2, causing broken/misleading referential integrity
No FK relationship to orders_v2 at all (relationship exists but is unenforced), so order_id values referencing orders_v2 rows aren't validated by the database
product_id has no enforced FK to products, allowing orphaned/nonexistent product references
order_id and product_id are nullable, permitting line items with no associated order or product
qty defaults to 1 but is nullable, allowing NULL quantities that break downstream sum/aggregate logic
unit_price_cents has no NOT NULL or CHECK constraint, allowing missing or negative prices
Table has 0 rows and 0 writes/day despite 41 reads/day, indicating readers may be querying a stale/empty table or the write path has moved elsewhere unnoticed

tables.doc: The `orders` table is a small, low-traffic (~2 rows) order-header table storing user_id, total, status, and creation timestamp. It is effectively deprecated: `order_items.order_id` still has an FK pointing here but the actual live order data has moved to `orders_v2`, so any consumer joining through `order_items` may be reading stale or orphaned rows here rather than current data.
issues: order_items -> orders FK is broken/stale: live order data now lives in orders_v2, so this table is likely deprecated but still referenced, risking silent reads of stale data
user_id is nullable despite an enforced FK to users, allowing orders with no owner
total is nullable numeric with no currency/unit column, and no CHECK constraint preventing negative values
status is an unconstrained free-text column with no enum/check constraint, allowing inconsistent or invalid values
created_at is nullable even though it defaults to now(), which can produce misleading null timestamps if the default is bypassed
table has only ~2 rows despite 41 reads/day, suggesting it may be near-unused test/legacy data rather than a real production table

tables.doc: orders_v2 stores order records (currently only ~5 rows, likely a low-volume or newly-migrated table) with amount in cents and a single-character status code defaulting to 'p' (presumably 'pending'). The '_v2' naming implies a prior 'orders' table was superseded, but no version/migration notes exist here, and none of the foreign keys (user_id, workspace_id) or inbound references (order_items, payments) are DB-enforced, so referential integrity relies entirely on application logic.
issues: No enforced foreign keys on user_id or workspace_id — orphaned orders possible if referenced users/workspaces are deleted
order_items.order_id and payments.order_id reference orders_v2 without enforced constraints — orphaned child rows possible if an order is deleted
status is an unconstrained free-text field defaulting to 'p' with no enum/check constraint or documented value set — high risk of typos and inconsistent codes over time

amount_cents stored as integer (cents) is fine for money-as-int, but no currency column exists — ambiguous for multi-currency support
created_at is nullable despite defaulting to now(), so backfilled/legacy rows could have NULL timestamps, breaking chronological assumptions
'_v2' suffix suggests a schema migration from a legacy 'orders' table with no documented cutover date or reconciliation status
meta jsonb column has no schema/validation, making its contents unpredictable across rows

tables.name: payments

columns.doc: Auto-incrementing primary key for the payment record.

columns.name: amount_cents

columns.name: state

columns.name: created_at

tables.doc: Tracks payment attempts/records tied to orders, keyed to Stripe events via stripe_event_id; at only ~3 rows and 3 writes/day this is likely a low-volume, possibly test/staging or newly-launched table. Amounts are stored in cents (integer) rather than a currency-aware money type, and the link to orders_v2 is a soft, unenforced relationship rather than a real foreign key. The 'orders_v2' naming suggests a prior orders table was replaced/migrated, which new engineers should be aware of when joining.
issues: order_id references orders_v2 but has no enforced foreign key, allowing orphaned payments if orders are deleted or IDs are mistyped
state is an unconstrained free-text column with no CHECK constraint or enum, risking inconsistent/typo'd status values (e.g. 'paid' vs 'Paid' vs 'succeeded')
stripe_event_id has no NOT NULL or UNIQUE constraint, so duplicate Stripe webhook deliveries could create duplicate payment rows
amount_cents, order_id, stripe_event_id, state, and created_at are all nullable despite being core to a payment record, allowing incomplete/garbage rows
created_at defaults to now() but there is no updated_at, so state transitions (e.g. pending -> succeeded) can't be audited or ordered in time
'orders_v2' naming implies a legacy/renamed orders table exists, creating ambiguity about which orders table is canonical

tables.doc: product_catalog_old is a legacy, near-dead product table (1 row, 0 reads/day, 1 write/day) that appears to be superseded by a newer product_catalog table; the 'old' suffix and abbreviated column names (pid, cat) signal deprecated naming conventions no longer used elsewhere. price stored as double precision (float) instead of a fixed-point/numeric/decimal type, risking rounding errors for monetary values
cat (category) is a free-text varchar with no FK to a categories table or enum constraint, allowing inconsistent/typo'd category values

tables.doc: The sessions table stores authentication session tokens linking users to active login sessions, with expiration timestamps used to enforce logout/timeout behavior. Despite an enforced FK to users, the table currently has zero rows and near-zero traffic (1 read/day, 0 writes/day), suggesting it may be unused, replaced by an external session store (e.g. Redis/JWT), or a dead/deprecated feature. Any new engineer or agent should verify whether this table is still the source of truth for auth before building on it.

tables.doc: Stores raw incoming Stripe webhook events, keyed by Stripe's event id, for auditing and idempotency checks before processing payment-related side effects. Extremely low volume (3 rows, ~3 writes/day) suggests this is either a new/low-traffic integration or events are being pruned/lost; the entire event payload lives in an unstructured jsonb blob with no derived columns for event type, processing status, or Stripe object id, so any consumer must parse payload to know what happened or whether it was handled.
issues: No 'event_type' or 'processing_status' column, so there's no way to query which events are unprocessed, failed, or duplicates without parsing jsonb payload
'payload' is nullable, allowing empty/placeholder rows that break the audit trail Stripe events are meant to provide
